blanks.sentence: Around _____ people will be affected by cancer in their lifetime.
Cancer involves cells growing out of control and causing _____.
In 2022, malignant cancers caused about _____ deaths worldwide.
Vaccines protect the body by making it _____ to a disease.
The development of mRNA is described as a sudden important _____.
Cancer can avoid attack by hiding from the body’s _____.
Cancer cells may put _____ on their surface to mislead the immune system.
Chemotherapy can attack the cancer but also damage _____.
New vaccines train the immune system in cancer-cell _____.
The aim of vaccines is the _____ of the immune system.

multipleChoice.question: How does the opening description distinguish benign from malignant tumours?
options: Benign tumours grow faster than malignant tumours.
Benign tumours are not cancerous, while malignant tumours are cancerous.
Benign tumours are always fatal, while malignant tumours are harmless.
Benign tumours affect only children, while malignant tumours affect adults.

multipleChoice.question: What basic function of vaccines is explained near the start?
options: They remove tumours through surgery.
They replace chemotherapy in every patient.
They make cancer cells grow more slowly.
They protect the body by creating immunity.

multipleChoice.question: Why does the immune system not automatically fight cancer effectively?
options: Cancer can hide from the body’s natural defences.
The immune system only works after chemotherapy.
Cancer cells are always outside the body’s tissues.
Vaccines make the immune system less active.

multipleChoice.question: What is the purpose of the “Go away! There’s nothing here to look at!” image?
options: To show that cancer cells communicate with doctors.
To suggest cancer can be removed by moving patients away.
To illustrate how cancer cells mislead the immune system.
To argue that immune therapy has failed over the past decade.

multipleChoice.question: Why is the phrase “Nothing to see here!” used in the explanation?
options: It explains how cancer hides by pretending there is no threat.
It warns that cancer research is impossible to observe.
It describes how police officers treat cancer patients.
It shows that healthy cells are more dangerous than cancer cells.

multipleChoice.question: In this context, what does it mean that cancer “hijacks” healthy cells?
options: It repairs healthy cells after chemotherapy.
It asks healthy cells to create vaccines.
It destroys all healthy cells immediately.
It takes control of something for its own advantage.

multipleChoice.question: How are existing treatments like chemotherapy contrasted with new vaccines?
options: Chemotherapy is natural, while vaccines damage healthy tissue.
Chemotherapy can harm healthy tissue, while vaccines aim to target cancer cells naturally.
Chemotherapy teaches the immune system, while vaccines directly attack all tissue.
Chemotherapy and vaccines work in exactly the same way.

multipleChoice.question: What problem does Professor Sanchez identify in the immune system of cancer patients?
options: It has become too aggressive against every healthy cell.
It refuses to respond to any form of treatment.
It has lost the ability to recognise cancer-cell abnormalities.
It attacks vaccines before they can enter the body.

multipleChoice.question: What does the vaccine try to do when the immune system is “blind” to cancerous growths?
options: Teach it to notice the danger and behave differently.
Make it ignore cancerous growths more completely.
Replace it with chemotherapy.
Stop it from recognising any abnormal cells.

multipleChoice.question: What broader conclusion is drawn about cancer treatments and vaccines?
options: Only vaccines should be used because other treatments no longer work.
Natural defences are useless once cancer has appeared.
Chemotherapy and vaccines must never be used together.
Different approaches may be used together or separately.
